source_refs.note: Topic 20.2.2 (PDF 157-160); Figures 20.2 to 20.5 are replaced by original diagrams.

items: DNA cleavage: the source DNA is cut with a restriction endonuclease and the gene of interest isolated; the vector DNA (plasmid or viral DNA) is cut with the same enzyme, so compatible sticky ends form on the gene and the vector.

Production of recombinant DNA: the cut vector and the gene are incubated together with DNA ligase, which joins them by phosphodiester linkages, so the vector becomes a recombinant vector carrying the gene.

blocks.alt: Top left: source DNA with a red gene of interest cut out at two restriction sites, giving the gene with sticky ends. Top right: a blue bacterial plasmid opened with the same enzyme. Below: the gene sealed into the plasmid by DNA ligase, forming a recombinant plasmid, which a bacterium takes up and copies as it divides.
blocks.caption: Making a recombinant plasmid and cloning it (original diagram after Figures 20.2 and 20.3).
blocks.long_description: The source DNA is cut with a restriction endonuclease to isolate the gene of interest, and the vector, here a plasmid, is cut with the same enzyme, so both carry compatible sticky ends. Incubated together with DNA ligase, the gene is inserted and sealed into the plasmid by phosphodiester bonds, making a recombinant plasmid. Bacteria in the same medium take up the recombinant DNA, and as they multiply they make clones carrying identical copies of the gene.

blocks.text: The recombinant vector and the expression system, usually bacteria, are incubated in the same medium and the bacterial cells take up the recombinant DNA. The bacteria multiply into clones that contain identical copies, clones, of the gene of interest.

items: Selecting for the vector (antibiotic resistance): the plasmid carries an antibiotic resistance gene, and the bacteria are grown on a medium containing that antibiotic (for example ampicillin), so only cells that took up a plasmid survive.

Selecting for the gene of interest (blue-white screening): the plasmid's lacZ' gene makes an enzyme that acts on a special sugar and turns it blue. A plain plasmid keeps lacZ' working and the colony turns blue; a successfully inserted gene breaks lacZ', so the desired recombinant colonies stay white.

blocks.alt: Left: three bacteria, one with no plasmid (killed by the antibiotic), one with a plain plasmid whose lacZ' gene works (blue colony), and one with a recombinant plasmid whose insert breaks lacZ' (white colony). Right: a plate with antibiotic and the special sugar, with blue and white colonies; a white colony is marked to keep.
blocks.caption: Antibiotic selection and blue-white screening (original diagram after Figure 20.4).
blocks.long_description: After transformation, the bacteria are grown on a medium containing an antibiotic such as ampicillin. The plasmid carries a gene for resistance to it, so only cells that took up a plasmid survive. To tell plain plasmids from recombinant ones the lacZ' gene of the plasmid is used: it makes an enzyme that acts on a special sugar in the medium and turns it blue. If the gene of interest has been inserted into lacZ' the gene is broken, so recombinant colonies stay white while colonies with a plain plasmid turn blue.

blocks.text: Identifying the specific gene (DNA hybridization): to confirm the gene is present a radioactive probe, a DNA strand complementary to the gene, is used. It hybridizes only with colonies containing the gene, and autoradiography with photographic film locates these colonies on the master plate.

blocks.alt: Five round plates in a row. 1: a master plate of white colonies. 2: a filter pressed on it holds a copy of the colonies. 3: cells broken and DNA strands separated. 4: a radioactive probe binds two colonies, marked with stars. 5: photographic film shows two dark spots, which point to the colonies to pick on the master plate.
blocks.caption: Finding colonies with the gene by hybridization (original diagram after Figure 20.5).
blocks.long_description: To confirm which colonies contain the gene of interest, a radioactive probe is used: a DNA strand complementary to the gene. The colonies are copied from the master plate onto a filter, the cells are broken open and their DNA made single-stranded, and the probe is added. It hybridizes only with colonies containing the gene, and autoradiography on photographic film shows where they are, so the matching living colonies can be picked from the master plate.

blocks.prompt: On a plate with ampicillin, which colonies do you pick: blue or white? Why?
blocks.explanation: White. Every colony that grows has a plasmid (ampicillin resistance), but only in white ones has the inserted gene broken lacZ', showing the plasmid is recombinant.

items: Cut gene and vector with the same enzyme; join with ligase.
Bacteria take up the vector and clone it.
Screen: antibiotic kills plasmid-free cells; white colonies are recombinant; a probe confirms the gene.
